lead: Every matrix, even a rectangular one, can be written as a rotation, a stretch along perpendicular axes, and another rotation. That is the singular value decomposition: A = UΣVᵀ. It exists for every real matrix, so it does what diagonalization does for symmetric matrices, but without needing A to be square or symmetric. Use it to compress data, solve ill-conditioned systems, fit least-squares models, and read rank. Exams usually ask you to compute the factors from AᵀA and to read rank and condition number from the singular values.
prereq: You need eigenvalues and the spectral theorem from Unit 4, and orthonormal vectors from chapter 5.3.

blocks.text: The SVD writes any real m × n matrix A as A = UΣVᵀ. U is m × m orthogonal, so UᵀU = I. V is n × n orthogonal, so VᵀV = I. Σ is m × n and has σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ 0 on its main diagonal; every other entry is zero. The numbers σᵢ are the singular values of A. Orthogonal matrices preserve lengths and angles, so U and V are rotations or reflections. Σ does the stretching: it multiplies the first coordinate by σ₁, the second by σ₂, and so on.

blocks.where: A is the m × n matrix being factorized; U is m × m orthogonal; Σ is m × n with σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ σ_min(m,n) ≥ 0 on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere; V is n × n orthogonal; Vᵀ is the transpose of V.

blocks.text: Why does this always work? The matrix AᵀA is n × n, real, and symmetric. Also xᵀAᵀA x = ||Ax||² ≥ 0, so AᵀA is positive semidefinite. By the spectral theorem from Unit 4, it has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors v₁,…,vₙ with real eigenvalues λ₁ ≥ … ≥ λₙ ≥ 0. Set σᵢ = √λᵢ. These are the singular values. For each σᵢ > 0 define uᵢ = Avᵢ/σᵢ. Then uᵢᵀuⱼ = (vᵢᵀAᵀAvⱼ)/(σᵢσⱼ) = (λⱼ vᵢᵀvⱼ)/(σᵢσⱼ) = 0 when i ≠ j, and 1 when i = j. So the uᵢ are orthonormal. If A has fewer nonzero singular values than m, fill the remaining columns of U with an orthonormal basis of the left null space, null(Aᵀ). Thus A = UΣVᵀ holds.
Compute an SVD in four steps.

items: Form AᵀA. It is n × n, symmetric, and positive semidefinite.
Find its eigenvalues λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ … ≥ λₙ ≥ 0 and choose orthonormal eigenvectors v₁,…,vₙ. Put them as columns of V.
Set σᵢ = √λᵢ. These go on the diagonal of Σ in the same order; zeros go after the positive values.
For each σᵢ > 0 set uᵢ = Avᵢ/σᵢ. If fewer than m such vectors appear, add an orthonormal basis of null(Aᵀ) to complete U.

blocks.text: The order matters. Column i of U, column i of V, and σᵢ belong to the same triple. If you reorder the singular values, reorder both columns in the same way. You may also compute A Aᵀ to get U directly; its nonzero eigenvalues are the same σᵢ². AᵀA is usually better for V because A has n columns.

items: Rank: rank A equals the number of nonzero singular values. Count σᵢ > 0, not the number of rows or columns.
Condition number: for a square invertible matrix, κ(A) = σ₁/σₙ. A large ratio means small input errors can become large solution errors. If σₙ = 0, the matrix is singular and κ is infinite.
Low-rank approximation: keeping only the first k terms, A ≈ σ₁u₁v₁ᵀ + … + σₖuₖvₖᵀ, gives the best rank-k approximation in the 2-norm (Eckart–Young).

figure.caption: The flow starts from the example matrix A, moves to AᵀA, then to V, then to the singular values 6.708 and 2.236, then to U, and ends at A = UΣVᵀ. Both singular values are nonzero, so the rank is 2.

spec.title: Computing the SVD for A = [[3,0],[4,5]]
spec.aria: A vertical flow from the example matrix A to A-transpose-A, then to its eigenvectors giving V, then to the singular values 6.708 and 2.236, then to the columns of U, and finally to the factorization with rank 2.

examples.question: Find the singular value decomposition of A = [[3,0],[4,5]]. Give U, Σ, V, the singular values to three decimal places, and rank A.
steps: Find eigenvalues from det(AᵀA − λI) = (25−λ)² − 20² = λ² − 50λ + 225 = 0. The roots are λ₁ = 45 and λ₂ = 5.
The singular values are σ₁ = √45 = 3√5 ≈ 6.708 and σ₂ = √5 ≈ 2.236. They are already in descending order.
For λ₁ = 45 solve (AᵀA − 45I)v = 0, giving v₁ = (1,1)/√2. For λ₂ = 5 solve (AᵀA − 5I)v = 0, giving v₂ = (1,−1)/√2. Thus V = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]].
Set Σ = diag(3√5, √5). Both singular values are nonzero, so rank A = 2. The product UΣVᵀ returns [[3,0],[4,5]].
examples.check:
import math
b11 = 3*3 + 4*4
b12 = 3*0 + 4*5
b22 = 0*0 + 5*5
tr = b11 + b22
det = b11*b22 - b12*b12
disc = tr*tr - 4*det
l1 = (tr + math.sqrt(disc))/2
l2 = (tr - math.sqrt(disc))/2
s1 = math.sqrt(l1)
s2 = math.sqrt(l2)
rank = (1 if s1 > 1e-12 else 0) + (1 if s2 > 1e-12 else 0)
print(round(s1, 9))
print(round(s2, 9))
print(rank)

traps: Taking eigenvalues of A itself instead of AᵀA. That shortcut is valid only for symmetric positive semidefinite matrices; A = [[0,1],[0,0]] has eigenvalues 0, 0 but singular values 1, 0.
Sorting singular values but not reordering U and V. The i-th column of U, the i-th column of V, and σᵢ form one triple.
Using only AᵀA when m > n and forgetting the left null space. U must be m × m, so fill missing columns with an orthonormal basis of null(Aᵀ).
Calling rank the number of rows, columns, or eigenvalues. Rank is the count of nonzero singular values.
Dividing by zero when σᵢ = 0. Leave that uᵢ out of the formula Avᵢ/σᵢ and complete U from the left null space; the condition number is infinite.

quiz.q: In A = UΣVᵀ for an m × n matrix A, state the sizes of U, Σ and V.
quiz.a: U is m × m orthogonal, Σ is m × n with singular values on the diagonal, and V is n × n orthogonal.

quiz.q: Why does AᵀA always have an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors?
quiz.a: AᵀA is real symmetric and positive semidefinite because xᵀAᵀAx = ||Ax||² ≥ 0. The spectral theorem gives real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis.

quiz.q: For A = [[2,0],[0,3]], find the singular values in descending order and rank A.
quiz.a: AᵀA = [[4,0],[0,9]], so eigenvalues are 9 and 4. σ₁ = √9 = 3, σ₂ = √4 = 2, and rank A = 2.

quiz.q: A 3 × 3 invertible matrix has singular values 8, 3 and 2. Find its 2-norm condition number.
A has σ₁ = 10 and σ₂ = 0.01. What does this imply about solving Ax = b, and about the best rank-1 approximation?
quiz.a: The condition number is 1000, so small errors in b can be amplified about 1000 times. The best rank-1 approximation keeps σ₁u₁v₁ᵀ and drops the small second term.

quiz.q: Give a 2 × 2 matrix whose eigenvalues are both 0 but whose singular values are 1 and 0. Why does this not contradict the SVD?
quiz.a: A = [[0,1],[0,0]] has characteristic polynomial λ², so eigenvalues 0, 0. But AᵀA = [[0,0],[0,1]] has eigenvalues 1, 0, so singular values 1, 0. The SVD uses AᵀA, not A; nonsymmetric matrices need not have singular values equal to eigenvalues.

beyond: Not for the exam. SVD drives principal component analysis, recommender systems, latent semantic analysis, and noise filtering. Practical libraries compute it by bidiagonalization and iterative QR, not by forming AᵀA, because forming AᵀA squares the condition number. Search next for Golub–Kahan SVD, Eckart–Young theorem, principal component analysis, and Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.
